blocks.x: We're recording this at Little Dad's house, Clarence Vincent's house. And today is January the what?
22nd.
21st.
21st.
Today is the 21st of January, by the Stonewall Jackson's birthday, 1960. And I guess we better get everybody's name here. Give me your name, huh?
What's your name? You. Clarence Vincent.
Okay, Punch?
Ernest Punch Miller.
Paul Crawford. And Dick Allen. Four of us, yeah. He wanted to talk about Bab Frank. Ask him about Bab.

So he wanted to talk about Bab Frank. I'll tell you a message I know about him. I was young then, you know. He had Bab Frank. He had a good band in his days, you know. He had a 70th band. He used to play all for these lawn parties, they called him at that time, yeah. And, uh, he was good at that time. He played a piccolo. Yeah, Kutcher Martin with him. Henry Martin. And I just remember who else he had, you know. But yeah, he was strong. He and John Robeshoe were the strongest one at that time, you know. For pinnacle, I mean for lawn parties, you know. And he'd serve people packing jams. Them children could go there at that time, you know, around my age. 11, 12, 14 with the parents, you know. And he used to always draw crowds, you know. Ask him what kind of band was it.
Was it a ragtime band or a reading band?

He said, was it a ragtime band or a reading band? Well, he was, he was, he was, Frank and Reed, but I don't know about Henry and Kutcher. I don't think I could read. But he had a good band, you know. He was a good band, you know. In them days, you know. It was a jazz, a rag band, you know. Ragtime? Yeah, ragtime band.
Ask him about Charlie McCurdy.
So how about Charlie McCurdy? Charlie McCurdy? Yeah, he had a good one too, yeah.
Did he, ask him, did he hear the Pillars?

Charlie McCurdy? Wait, let me see. George McCurdy's the man, huh? Yeah. Now, Charlie? Did he play? Soft. Soft. So he played soft. Oh, Charlie, yeah. Charlie used to play with me. But he never did own a band. He used to play with John Robeshoe's band. And that's why I was playing with him. And then from there, Louis the man got him. But he was so soft. After he got off the clarinet, he got on sack. And we thought by him getting on sack, he would blow loud, but it was the same thing. He did kick in, but he was a musician at all. And he learned Walter Blondie how to play clarinet, you know. And that's how Walter Blondie got me with them. You know, John Robeshoe's band. I stayed with them, the people didn't hire him no more. Then the people come out to hire me, well, that's taking them with me, you know. He had died out then, you know. Yeah, Charlie McCurdy. I was thinking about John McCurdy.
Well, I asked him, did he hear the Peerless band?
He said, did you ever hear the Peerless band? The Peerless.
I don't know.
It wasn't Peer Calico, was it? No, Peerless. Peerless. Peerless, Peerless band. Oh, I heard tack of that, but I just remember that.
That's Bab Frank and Charlie McCurdy.
Bab Frank and Charlie McCurdys. Yeah, yeah. You know, that's what he should call it band. That's how he should call it, Bab Frank's band, you know. But that's where they band then.
When you were about 12 years old, you have here on the sheet. A sheet of paper. What about August Roussel?

What about August Roussel? August Roussel used to play with us too. He was a tambour player. He was a good leader too, but sometimes he used to make mistakes and Lewis the Man, he used to get after him all the time, you know. I played with him about three years. But it wasn't his band, it was Lewis the Man's band. And we had Gus Muscapper and Robert Hall. You heard talking about Robert Hall? Edward Hall's brother. We had a line up like that. We had Henry Rush with us once. When he quit, we had Joe Stratton. You ever tell you about Joe Stratton? Go ahead. I believe he's dead now, yeah. What did he play? Drummer. Yeah, he died in Chicago. Yeah. Joe Stratton. Yeah, Joe Stratton, yeah. He's a good drummer. He used to play with them. He was the best around there. He's the best in Chicago too.
Slide whistle, you mean? Yeah. And Henry Rush was playing drums at the time?

Henry Rush was playing drums at the time? Yeah. He got off the drum and went on cornet. Now he's on bass. If he's playing bass violin, you know. I ain't seen him about three or four years. It's really long, isn't it? He live over the river now.
Did you have Gus Mudcat and August Russel at the same time?

Did you have Gus Mudcat and August Russel at the same time? Was I playing with him? Yeah, same time. Yeah, you know. You see, Gus had that band. And when Gus died, Louis took it in his name. You see, Louis the man band.
And who did Louis take on trombone when Gus died?
Who did Louis take on trombone when Gus died?
August, August Russel. I see.
Yeah.
Couldn't get that straight.

I was still with him, you know. We went to Sweetsburg State about two months over there. But they couldn't measure. They couldn't pass with the farmer. Every gentleman, you know, and come back there. You see?
Well, ask him about what year was this?
He said about what year was this? When you was with Louis the man. I see. It's kind of hard.
Ask him if it was before World War II, Ponce.

Was it before World War II? Yeah, yeah. Before that. You see, when I was there, I don't know what I mean. I can't hide more than any banjo or guitar player in the city. Everybody wants me to play with them, you know. And I used to play with them, but my band wasn't doing nothing. But when I was over there in Sweetsburg, they was just waiting for me to come back so they could tell me to Florida. Let me see what part that was, what part of Florida? Mommy's Florida. And then I told him about my friend, Manny Sears. Yeah, I told you, yeah, man. What, Manny, what you want to go in there? Oh, Manny Sears. He used to pack his every day, but he wasn't playing with no band. So I looked back and told him to see if he could get him to go. So they got him. And they told me, man, you sent us a good banjo player. And he is good. He's good, yes. Everybody wanted me. I don't know how. There's plenty of fellas that beat me playing too, you know. And still, you know, they come, they want me to play with them. I used to be good all the time. Sometimes I had to tell them fellas, you know, I was tired. I had to tell them, much like I was playing, you know. And always be there, somebody just suddenly plays, you know, in my place.
Ask me if he was playing with Louis Dumaine after he went to Mexico or before he went to Mexico.

Was you playing with Louis Dumaine before you went to Mexico or after? Or before I went to Mexico. Yeah. Because we had some, we were speaking to some, I tell you, two husbands. First we wanted Commitator. You know why I talk to her. We wanted her because she was a musician. And them bands, there was one of all them bands away from the sweet sports. All of them were four or five piece bands. So they tried to knock it to the white people that, we had a good band but they read them old notes. And the white people were the right time music, you know. And so when they went to get out to old man Lovenson, he told me, he said, I got two little shorts fellas in that band. And he said, we're trying to get the piano playing. If you didn't have no piano playing over there, you didn't have no band, you know. And so well then after they looked into it, Lovenson told me, he said, I'll give you a try. He said, I'll make, I'll make you turn that band, that piano around with those two little shorts fellas I can say. Banjo playing in a bass. That's a mean chesty, you know. Yeah. And then when we went over there, ooh, the white people like to throw it down, you know, those little young students. And all of them got together and turned the piano around. He said, Lovenson, you got a band. But you see, the job wasn't regular over there. It was just like a hustling job. You see, the white people are higher, but they're going to give something like that. And then we had to get on the road, go from state to state. Sometime we make five, sometime we make four, sometime we make two. On a holiday, we make around about ten dollars. But we couldn't make it that time because the people there were charging so much for bone and large, you see. And you know, it was cold in the sweet port when it was cold. Beans, snow, everything. And those people had one little thin blanket. Gas, we were scared of food, the gas on the counter, you know, we were dirty. We stood there about three months with him and we jumped in, you know, and come back here. I don't know.
What about, what about Bud Russel or Bud Russell?
What about Bud Russell? Bud Russell?
Bass player. Bass player.

Oh, Bud Russel. Russel. Yeah, he, you see, I got to spell it wrong, isn't it? Bud Russel. But he had a band a long time. You remember a boy, don't you, Bud Russel? Bass player. Oh, he had different bands, you know. And he used to get all those youngsters like me, George McCullum. Little young fellas, you know, would play. And we kept him up. He always get a good band. He kept up to, he couldn't play no more, you know. Went to work, things got data on there. He'd get plenty of work through it. How long has he been dead?
How long has he been dead? How long has he been dead? My brother must be dead about, um.

You see, my belly, my belly, I'm saying. See, time passed up, but my belly been dead about 23 years. I think Bud died before him. That's why his niece was two years old when my belly died. My brother died, George. You remember my brother George? He was a psycho. He wasn't much a musician, but he was, you know, make out sometimes, you know. He'd take a chance anyway, you know. Just better work, too. Yeah, I was all them boys. Lee Collins and, um, Lee Collins and, uh, Kid Rene. Oh, Bud Appetite. They all used to go with him on the job. He said, well, I ain't gonna have much of that money, cause you get a good price for your work. So, who worked with Bud Russel? I used to work with him sometimes. I worked with him a long time. George McCullum and, uh, let me see what, and, uh, Mike Williams. I got him on there, too. He was a kind of player. And, uh, let me see what I was. Sometimes, Earl Humphrey used to work with him. You know, he'd just have a mix-up band. Whoever would get high, you know. You know, he was kind of crooked sometimes with the money, you know. Ask him about the... He'd just say, Bud, touch the box sometimes, you know. You know, they did get a good line-up, too, Bud did. Uh, I used to play at the Lake, you know, we were doing probation then, you know. And we played, uh, at, uh, Devon Spring, you know, over in Coventry. And we played out there and the white people give us cold, red and a whiskey, you know, and drink. And Bud wanted, Bud wanted to be the boss of us, you know. Bud he'd be a joy, you know. And every time he wanted to drink, he'd give us a little, you know. And he wanted to pack it over for his wife, you know. His wife used to like play there. And me and George, we come and watch him one day, see where he's hiding. And we went there, and we got my three full Coca-Cola bottles. And we poured all the gin out in there, and then poured water in there and put it back. And then, uh, these guys got hands, I got there, you know. But Bud didn't know where we been getting it from. So Bud came to know, he said, Baby, I got some real stuff for you. I said, when they take it, take it, he said, Bud, are you crazy or what? And she talked about all this Bud, hey. There was nothing in there but spring water. And Bud didn't know who did it, you know. They tell him, you know.
Did you play with Bud before he was with the Liberty Bell or after?

He said, did you play with Bud before he was with the Liberty Bell or after? Before he was with the Liberty Bell. Before you was with the Liberty Bell. No, the Liberty Bell band was my band. I put Brunt, Josh Brunt, the manager of it, you know. But it was my band, I organized our band.
I asked him which came first.

We had some band, too. Most of our jobs called for white people. We said. We was up three years before we could play for one color people. And the first time we played for color people when Joe Oliver left from the air. You know, the thing I got in there when I was standing right by Joe Oliver with a fellow drumming him, Buddy Sali. Hit him in the eye with a wheel by the hammer. And you know, I thought Joe would be one eye, you know. And he used to have a man, Carol, all them boys. He must have been around about seventeen, eighteen years old. All of them were like that. And they would take me, well, into Bad New York. I didn't know how to play no music then, you know. I just used to follow them around. Wasn't nothing but boys that time. And they had a good band, but it was a brass band, you know. And a brother named Kinson had that band, you know. And he showed the people how he could bring these little youngses up, you know. Then way after that, then, where Lewis Armstrong come out of John's womb. That's where Lewis learned, too. And me and Lewis sometimes used to go down, this is called them tunks. He got on there and wait for Bunk Johnson. And Bunk used to like to drink, you know. And he used to, you know, buy us a little drink. Me and Henry Roy. Well, that's where Lewis learned all these good stuff from Bunk Johnson, you see, after he come out of home. Then when Joe Oliver found out that Lewis was so good, he sent for him. And Lewis went up there, some piano player they had. And they found out Lewis was so good that Joe used to tell him to blow, blow low, you know. Blow under him. And so the piano player, she was a woman, I forget the name. Lil! Huh? Lil! Yeah, well she got, she got, uh, uh, Lewis off the side and told him, say, Lewis, everybody say you can beat Joe Oliver, blow his chords. Said, I feel like Joe keeps you down. I say, make sure you forget to blow over him. Mm-hmm. And old Lewis did that. And, uh, come out the days after the, where everybody would just scream hot and clap. But Lewis Armstrong would blow over Joe. And that's where Lewis got to be the famous of the war, you see. I tell you, Joe was good, Joe. Yeah, he was alright. Yeah. And that's where Lewis could beat him then. Lewis was just coming out good then, you know. And then Guy Kelly, he went up there with Guy, he said Guy Kelly, drink, you know. He said, drink, yeah. And he said, I don't like me and stuff. Bad, you know, bootlegger. That must have hit Guy Kelly's stomach up. When we came to Guy, we had a special glass, that's a big glass. And got it, . And he would play. You see, Allen, Fred Allen, he didn't drink. Let me drink now, you know, some part of the chain. And we couldn't get Fred Allen to leave his daddy. Every job we go on his daddy had to be there. That's where he got me to join his band. And that's just a rotten band. I said, Allen, I said, you're a good corny player. I said, but you ain't got no backers. I said, that holds me back too. I said, I don't want to come in here and break up your band. So he said, but can you get me some good man? I said, I get you man. I said, you hate this townskip. I got him one of my little friends, Albert Martin. He's there too. Remember Albert Martin? Yeah. Yeah, he's there too. And I got him George Lewis. He was a first climber. Got him him. And I got Ellis got on the bass. And let me see what I say. Let me see. Drum, bass, guitar, and trombone. I got Bourne. Bourne was the weakest man in the island band, but he could make out. You see, all of us was over Bourne. And Bourne didn't know no music. And then we had the bass band around there. The kids were there. Every time we played for a dance, people would be like that. Couldn't get in. And we stayed up after the time. You know, it was time 26. 1926 when I went to Mexico. That's where my mom was.
I asked you who this Bourne was. That's not Harrison Bourne.
That's been about 24 years ago, ain't it? Is that Harrison Bourne? Huh? Is that Harrison Bourne, you mean? Harrison? Bourne. Uh, Julius Bourne. Julius Bourne. Julius Bourne.
He couldn't be Harrison.

He was from Morgan City. He used to be around there. He left them here and went to Alexander. I went to play with him in Alexander, but I stayed over there four years. And then people don't pay nothing. Only go from state to state. Make 15 cents. Time is bad over there then. You can ride on a free train for nothing. Go anywhere for nothing, you know, looking for weight. Sometimes we go to Texas. A great big white brother, about six feet tall, a little over, and great big hats on. They come to me. They wouldn't call me Shawty. They said, well, my boy, he said, what you over here with a circus? I said, no, sir Cap. I said, you over here with a band. He said, band? I said, well, these niggas over here, you got nothing? He said, we feed you. The guy said, yeah, the doctor, go in there. Let's go and get something neat. I know you're hogging. And I was hogging too, man. He said, you only gonna make nothing. So we went to the mile at a time. And the mile at a time, said, what do I want? I said, we want to get a permit. He said, why you getting money to get a permit? He said, we could say after the day, they go and give us a day. He said, you only gonna make nothing. They give us a dollar, you know, so we should go to the restaurant and get something to eat. He said, we're taking care of these people over here. He said, they ain't got nothing. And sure enough, that night, there was one death in Dermotville to pay two bits. And we just played. We looked out there, it looked like they had about 3,000 people out there. Stand up and listen, you know. And they all could be one death in Dermotville. We could have it hard. Remember, we went to Longview, Texas. There was a John Tonkin there. Had a 14-piece band. We went over there, and the fella gave us the hall to play. We had about 15 or 20 people in there. They didn't know where to stay, so the fella let us stay in there. And when we stayed in there, you know, so... And when we stayed in there, we stayed in there all night. And another fella in there blow the woman's head, keen off from my, you know, from my body. And we ain't never woke up until the people come in there and woke us up. And when we woke up, we were surprised. Didn't even hear the shotgun. They fed us too, you know. Our time was hard.
Ask him about Joe Harris, Winston.

Say, how about Joe Harris? Joe Harris, he just used to play with a different fella. He's a good sucker for her. He was a good sucker for her. He was a good sucker for her. He wasn't talking to me. He wasn't out there yet. He wasn't good at that sucker for her. He was a good sucker for her.
Ask him what kind of...

He played with different bands too then. He was playing... A long time I heard from him was playing with Earl Foster. You know Earl Foster. We played with him. I played with Earl. A long time too. Ooh, long time too.
Ask him did he play clarinet too?
So did he play clarinet too? Who?
Joe Harris.
Joe Harris. No, no, I don't think Leslie just could play a little. Ever since I first started him was on a sax.
Alto or baritone? Alto?
Huh? Alto sax or baritone? Yeah, alto. He played alto.
Ask him any other bands he worked with.
Who's the other bands he worked with? Who was the other bands he worked with? Joe Harris. Joe Harris. Oh, he worked with plenty bands. He used to work with our tape.
And he wants to talk about it.
I said he used to work with different bands, and there was a regular job in a beer garden, you know? Clubs like that, you know.
Ask him about Eddie Hickman. He asked him.

How's about Eddie Hickman? Eddie Hickman, well Eddie Hickman, he had a band. He had George McCullum, he had Artie Crasman, and he had Max Williams, and he had Little Lawrence, Little Lawrence Coleman, and Gitar, no, Gitar, yeah. He's dead too. I believe Eddie's dead too. I read in the paper last week if it's him, you know, Eddie Hickman, you know. It wasn't. I don't know. Oh, you don't know him, man. He's an old musician too. This shot fella, he wasn't much taller than me. He gets mad quick. He's a nice liquor too. He's a fine liquor that fella. He gets mad so quick. Yeah, he had a band a long time too. He used to get that smart way. Remember that time he was running the million back at the St. Jude, and had them two bands? I don't remember. You remember that? Yeah, he had Chris Jackson, yeah, that's what he did. You know when two bands play against one another? I remember them bands play against one another. You don't remember that? What's the name of that band? Huh? What was the name of his band? What's the name of Eddie Hickman's band? I played crosswinds with him. Yeah, when you played back there, you know, when you didn't play like you played with Jack, you know. You played the straight corner at just a little chair. And people gave us, I was with you then, the people gave us the decedent over there. Yeah, we won, you see. Damn boy, you can know something. I bet that Dave remember that. Damn, I don't know Octave. Yeah, yeah.
You don't know Octave?
No, what did he play? Yeah, I played at the Palace.

Octave Frost. Yeah, left on the picture. Can't you see him in the picture? Mm-hm. That's him. Yeah, I might have known him. Working there now. Well, you never worked at the paddock recently? How much had you had a few nights at Punch?
The paddocks? I didn't play there for one night.
And who was the piano player? You don't remember? It might have been him. Must have been. Mm-hm.
I don't know who was there. I didn't believe there was one night.
And who was the piano player? You don't remember?
Might have been him.
Must have been.
I don't know who was there. What the old client of the piano is?
Piku? Piku. Yeah, well, it's been Octave.
Been a good while ago.
What about Willie Hightower?

What about Willie Hightower? He's been, uh, you might have known him after Chicago. I know him, yeah. Well, he used to play with different fellows. He used to get that trumpet player too, before he left here, you know. The kid used to play around with different fellows, you know. Ask him, did he play ragtime?
He went to Chicago.
So did he play ragtime? Yeah, yeah, he used to play ragtime. I was trying to remember if he could read it, you know. Very few of them was reading then. Yeah, he wasn't about to have him.
What about Lorenzo Stahl?
See, what about Lorenzo Stahl? See, Banzo playing guitar. See, didn't you all talk about him, huh?
Yeah, I know what a dirty mouth he had. He's my mouth, don't you?

Yeah. He was a dirty fellow. Talk dirty. Yeah, he had the women, 30 women. They'd be crazy about it. Yeah. A towel across his shoulder. What, a towel across his shoulder? Yeah. Why? He used to find him to come get me, you know. He used to ask me what I'm playing. I said, I don't want to tell you anything. He's a son, my buddy. And I didn't want to tell you, but they said he wasn't playing with him no more. Well, I would go with him, you know. What band was that? Well, he was tired of. So what band was that? What he used to play with? Let me see what band was that. That was Franky Dushy left. Yeah, I should've been playing with him for a long time. But to see Franky Dushy… Seltzer. I hate the ball. It's a man, we didn't want to see. Well, yeah.
How about Buddy Salo?
The drummer.
The drummer.
Yeah.
Who hit Joe Oliver?
Buddy Salo. Buddy Salo? Yeah. That's the one that hit Joe Lewis. Joe Oliver. Yeah. And what Joe Lewis? Joe Oliver. Oliver. Joe Oliver.
Ask him, did he play after that?
Did we play after that? He come down there, you know, and play a little while. He didn't live long. He went into consumption, you know.
Who did he play with?

Who did he play with? Just some fellas down there. I wasn't playing music then, you know. He'd play class, you know, victory balls, you know. All of them trunks, you know. I don't know. I could play manolene a little bit. The amount that I learned good when I used to play with Clarence Williams, you know. Piano, manolene, violin, and sax. That was Cindy Bessier. Yeah, he was, Cindy was a good thing. Cindy was a good thing. Cindy used to play with anybody too. You know, when he was cold out. Yeah, he didn't have any band. My band, he could buy Clarence for Cindy. Give him Cindy. Yeah, he cared about Cindy. Ask him if you ever worked with Mike Murray. Mike Murray? Yeah, the drummer. So, did you ever work with Mike Murray, the drummer? Yeah.
He's trying to make the sax. He's a drummer.
Yeah.
So, he's a drummer.
Mac Murray. Mac Murray. Mac Murray. Yeah. He's the drummer. Yeah. He's the drummer. Mac Murray. Mac Murray. Mac Murray. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. I can't remember much more. Old, old. I know one father, I forget his name. You know him? You seen him personally? He works at the National Bank on Camp and Night. I'm in a magazine at night. I just remember he lived. I played with him a couple of times. But Mike Murray, I don't know how.
What about Abe Buller, the trumpet player?
What's that name?
Abe Buller, I guess.

Abe Buller, what trumpet player? What about him? Abe? Bully. Bully. From Baton Rouge. From Baton Rouge. From Baton Rouge. Oh, that's when I chose to play with the Hill City Bears. East Flat. East Flat Cornet. I wasn't playing with him today. Then when I went to Baton Rouge, after I got older, I know him good. He was the uncle of my friend. We'd come up together, you know. That's why I know all them fathers in Baton Rouge.
Ask him what his name is.

What is his real name? What is his real name? Abraham Burdenhill. Abraham Burdenhill. Abraham Burdenhill. You know where it is? Burdenhill. This is with Walter Burke. And you know the Hill City Bears.
Ask him was a Hill City Band a brass band or a dance band or both?
He said was a Hill City Band a brass band or a dance band or both? Brass band and some of the men out of there just had my eyes to say.
Ask him who else Mike Williams played with?

He said who else Mike Williams played with? Well he played with Lattes, George McCullum. Just a little bands I got him in. He had got office once here at Lockjaw. And he stayed office so long after me and him got together, you know, he tried to get his comeback. He never could, but he could make out for the fair, you know. We should get a little jobs and work together, you know. What about Willie Warner?
What about Willie Warner?
Willie Warner? I said you never know him, eh? You know where you talk about Willie Warner?
Yeah, I heard talk about him.

Oh, yeah. He used to play with people. And then he played with us. And then he played with George Williams, big George Williams. Then he had a band, you know. Boy, he played with Peerrell until Peerrell died. Then after that, he didn't spend with anybody, you know. Work all the time. He was a printer, you know. Played music at night. He was a heavy drinker. He was the finest man in one of me. He didn't look at him up there. I used to play with him sometimes too. Me and him and Eddie Hickman. Three piece. He could play too. What about Hippolyte? He was kind of settled, I think. So what about Hippolyte? Hippolyte Charles. Hippolyte Charles used to play. I used to play with Hippolyte Charles. He was player on band number two. Hippolyte Charles. Hippolyte Charles. Kermitra Charles. Reddigger. Rabbit Hole. Myself. I don't know who she has. I think Oak was a bit of trombone with him.
Oak? Oak.
I can't ask him. Oh, Vic. Yeah. Vic. Vic. Vic.

segments.chapter: Opening and the early lawn-party bands
segments.title: Recording setup and introductions at Vincent's house
segments.summary: The interviewer states the date, 21 January 1960, and the four people present: Vincent, Punch Miller, Paul Crawford and Dick Allen. Miller relays questions, starting with Bab Frank.

segments.chapter: Opening and the early lawn-party bands
segments.title: Bab Frank's ragtime lawn-party band
segments.summary: Vincent recalls Bab Frank's band playing lawn parties when he was 11 to 14, with Henry Martin and Kutcher Martin, and says it was a ragtime band whose players mostly could not read.

segments.chapter: Opening and the early lawn-party bands
segments.title: Charlie McCurdy, John Robichaux's band and the Peerless band
segments.summary: Vincent describes Charlie McCurdy as a soft clarinet and sax player who never led a band but played in John Robichaux's band, and who taught Walter Blondie. The Peerless band is identified as Bab Frank's and McCurdy's band.

segments.chapter: Opening and the early lawn-party bands
segments.title: August Roussel, Gus Mudcat and Louis Dumaine's band
segments.summary: Vincent played about three years in the band led by Louis Dumaine. It had August Roussel on trombone, Gus Mudcat, Robert Hall, and drummers Henry Rush and Joe Stratton, and Louis took over the band when Gus died.

segments.chapter: Opening and the early lawn-party bands
segments.title: Out-of-town job with Louis Dumaine's band and getting Manny Sears hired
segments.summary: Vincent remembers a roughly two-month trip out of the city before World War II with Louis Dumaine's band, and recommending banjoist Manny Sears for a Florida job. He says every band wanted him.

segments.chapter: Bud Russell, the Liberty Bell band and the road
segments.title: Playing for Lovenson and the hard road job before going to Mexico
segments.summary: Vincent describes a three-month stretch with Lovenson's small band, which won over white audiences. The money was poor and the travel hard, with five, four or two dollars a night and cold lodging, after which they came back.

segments.chapter: Bud Russell, the Liberty Bell band and the road
segments.title: Bud Russell's bands, his sidemen and the spiked gin prank
segments.summary: Vincent talks about bassist Bud Russell, who led mixed bands of young players such as George McCullum and Mike Williams, was sometimes crooked with money, and was the target of a prank where Vincent and George swapped his gin for water.

segments.chapter: Bud Russell, the Liberty Bell band and the road
segments.title: The Liberty Bell band, Joe Oliver, young Armstrong and Fred Allen's band
segments.summary: Vincent says the Liberty Bell band was his own. In one long answer he tells how Buddy Sali hit Joe Oliver in the eye, how Armstrong learned from Bunk Johnson and then outblew Oliver, and how he built a band for Fred Allen before going to Mexico in 1926.

segments.chapter: Bud Russell, the Liberty Bell band and the road
segments.title: Julius Bourne and the hard barnstorming years in Texas
segments.summary: After identifying Julius Bourne of Morgan City, Vincent recalls four years on the road, playing for tiny pay, riding free trains, sleeping in a hall in Longview, Texas, and a crowd of about 3,000 at a small-town dance.

segments.chapter: Musicians the interviewers ask about
segments.title: Joe Harris, alto saxophonist who worked with many bands
segments.summary: Vincent says Joe Harris played alto sax, not clarinet, worked with Earl Foster and many other bands, and played regular beer-garden jobs.

segments.chapter: Musicians the interviewers ask about
segments.title: Eddie Hickman's band, a battle of bands and Octave Frost
segments.summary: Vincent and Punch Miller recall Eddie Hickman's band and its sidemen, including George McCullum, Max Williams and Lawrence Coleman, and a contest between two bands. They then try to place pianist Octave Frost.

segments.chapter: Musicians the interviewers ask about
segments.title: Willie Hightower, who played ragtime and went to Chicago
segments.summary: Vincent recalls Willie Hightower playing with different groups before leaving for Chicago, and playing ragtime, though few could read it then.

segments.chapter: Musicians the interviewers ask about
segments.title: Lorenzo Staulz, guitarist with a dirty mouth and many women
segments.summary: Vincent remembers Lorenzo Staulz as a banjo and guitar player who talked dirty and had many women, and tries to recall which band he played in.

segments.chapter: Drummers, trumpeters and Baton Rouge
segments.title: Buddy Sali, the drummer who hit Joe Oliver
segments.summary: Vincent confirms that drummer Buddy Sali was the one who hit Joe Oliver. Sali played a while afterward but died young of consumption.

segments.chapter: Drummers, trumpeters and Baton Rouge
segments.title: Playing with Clarence Williams, and drummer Mike Murray
segments.summary: Vincent says he learned mandolin well while playing with Clarence Williams and mentions Cindy Bessier. The interviewers then ask about drummer Mike Murray, whom Vincent can barely recall.

segments.chapter: Drummers, trumpeters and Baton Rouge
segments.title: Trumpeter Abe Buller of Baton Rouge and the Hill City Bears
segments.summary: Vincent identifies the Baton Rouge trumpeter as Abraham Burdenhill, whom he knew through the Hill City Bears, a brass band, and through a friend's family.

segments.chapter: Drummers, trumpeters and Baton Rouge
segments.title: Mike Williams and the small bands Vincent got him into
segments.summary: Vincent says Mike Williams played with George McCullum and the small bands Vincent put him in, and tried a comeback after a long layoff.

segments.chapter: Drummers, trumpeters and Baton Rouge
segments.title: Willie Warner, Hippolyte Charles and Vic
segments.summary: Vincent describes Willie Warner as a printer who played at night and worked with big George Williams and Eddie Hickman. He recalls playing with Hippolyte Charles's band and Oak's brother Vic, who had a weak heart.

segments.chapter: Drummers, trumpeters and Baton Rouge
segments.title: A musician still strong, playing with Kid Thomas on January 3
segments.summary: The interviewer says a musician Vincent has just discussed played with Kid Thomas on 3 January. Vincent says he used to be strong and drew plenty of work.

segments.chapter: Casa, Zeb Lenard and Little Joe
segments.title: Red Happy, the loud drummer, and the Eureka Band
segments.summary: Vincent recalls drummer Red Happy as terrible but good, someone who died in Chicago. The interviewer says he is still with the Eureka Band.

segments.chapter: Casa, Zeb Lenard and Little Joe
segments.title: The Casa, a friend killed on the way to a gig, and a pay dispute
segments.summary: Vincent recalls playing the Casa. He tells of a friend killed by a car before he could start a band, and of a leader paying him and John Casimir eight dollars a night while drummer Mason got more.

segments.chapter: Casa, Zeb Lenard and Little Joe
segments.title: Ernest Kelly, uniforms and diabetes
segments.summary: Asked why Zeb and Ernest Kelly are linked, Vincent recalls Ernest Kelly's size, the uniform tailor's charge, his diabetes and death, and that he went to Mexico with them.

segments.chapter: Casa, Zeb Lenard and Little Joe
segments.title: Zeb Lenard, Buddy Petit and George Lewis's early bands
segments.summary: Vincent says Zeb worked with Buddy Petit and Jack, and that Petit left for Chicago. George Lewis worked with Vincent more than with any band and also with Petit and Kid Howard.

segments.chapter: Casa, Zeb Lenard and Little Joe
segments.title: Albert Martin, taken from one band and put in Vincent's
segments.summary: Vincent says he took Albert Martin out of another band and into his own. After Vincent went to Mexico the band separated and Albert went to Texas.

segments.chapter: Casa, Zeb Lenard and Little Joe
segments.title: Teaching Little Joe the trumpet, and his later troubles
segments.summary: Vincent taught the 14-year-old Little Joe to play horn by picking his banjo, within four months Joe could blow. He tells of Joe's marijuana and whiskey habits, his later breakdown and turn to preaching, and chats about where they live.

segments.chapter: Casa, Zeb Lenard and Little Joe
segments.title: Kid Shots, cornetist who deputised for Little Joe
segments.summary: Vincent calls Kid Shots a good cornet player who liked whiskey and filled in for Little Joe for two weeks. He says dance-hall rules about children hurt their work.

segments.chapter: Wooden Joe's band and Sidney Correa
segments.title: Albert Nicholas in Paris and Danny Barker
segments.summary: Vincent recalls Albert Nicholas, now in Paris, and says he played one job with Danny Barker.

segments.chapter: Wooden Joe's band and Sidney Correa
segments.title: Wooden Joe's band, John Tassel and its trombonist and drummer
segments.summary: Vincent played in Wooden Joe's band, which was really John Tassel's, and says Joe had an earlier band. He tries to recall its trombone player, linked to Brother Petit's father, and its drummer.

segments.chapter: Wooden Joe's band and Sidney Correa
segments.title: Sidney Correa and the bands they played in together
segments.summary: Vincent recalls playing a long time with Sidney Correa, whose brother was a classical player, and tries to name the band, settling on trombonist Raymond Brown. Mixed bands of neighbours were common.

segments.chapter: Wooden Joe's band and Sidney Correa
segments.title: Pinchback, a teacher who could not play, and playing fast for white dancers
segments.summary: Vincent talks about Pinchback as a teacher who could not execute the instrument. He says white dancers once wanted fast music, and mentions Isaiah Morgan and Tranchina's 400-pound frame.

segments.chapter: Banjo career, Armstrong and the Liberty Bell
segments.title: Tranchina's demand that Vincent read banjo parts, and the five-flat piece
segments.summary: Vincent tells how Tranchina took over the banjo to show him up and fired a band. He was brought in with Louis Dumaine, read the music in five flats without a mistake, and won Tranchina's praise.

segments.chapter: Banjo career, Armstrong and the Liberty Bell
segments.title: Tony Jackson, the solo pianist, and drummer Bruno Joseph
segments.summary: Vincent remembers Tony Jackson as a well-known solo piano player who did not play with bands. He then describes drummer Bruno Joseph, who died after drinking bad corn whiskey.

segments.chapter: Banjo career, Armstrong and the Liberty Bell
segments.title: Trombonist Eddie Vincent, who shares his name
segments.summary: Asked about Eddie Vinson, Vincent says he met him in Chicago, noted that they share a name, and could not place him otherwise.

segments.chapter: Banjo career, Armstrong and the Liberty Bell
segments.title: Big Eye Louis, Buddy Christian and a recent carnival-day job
segments.summary: Vincent says he played with Big Eye Louis but did not know his father. He tells of a recent carnival job with a young sax player, and says Buddy Christian played house parties and learned chords by guiding other players' fingers.

segments.chapter: Banjo career, Armstrong and the Liberty Bell
segments.title: Where Louis Armstrong got his style
segments.summary: Vincent credits Bunk Johnson and what Armstrong learned at the Home, and repeats how Joe Oliver kept him down until a piano player urged him to blow over Oliver.

segments.chapter: Banjo career, Armstrong and the Liberty Bell
segments.title: How the Liberty Bell band got its name
segments.summary: Vincent says he chose the name from novels he read about the Liberty Boys of '76. The band became popular and its alumni became known worldwide.

segments.chapter: Bands, arranging and other players
segments.title: Amos White, and a Creole jazz band job that ended in a brawl
segments.summary: Vincent talks about Amos White, then tells of his Creole jazz band playing a rough job where drunken patrons turned on them, and the band left with about $35 each.

segments.chapter: Bands, arranging and other players
segments.title: Members of the Kid Albert and Barnes band
segments.summary: Vincent lists the six men in the Kid Albert and Barnes band, including Joe Struttis, Ory Foster and himself, and says they played for a Jewish organisation.

segments.chapter: Bands, arranging and other players
segments.title: Arranging in the old bands and Louis Dumaine's violin parts
segments.summary: Vincent says he and a partner arranged for their own band. Lewis Dumaine could read from a violin part, play it upside down or transposed, and supply cornet and trombone parts without writing them.

segments.chapter: Bands, arranging and other players
segments.title: Tats Alexander and his father Adolph Alexander, arranger for Celestin
segments.summary: Vincent identifies Tats Alexander as a downtown reed player whose father, Adolph Alexander Sr., a trumpeter, arranged for Celestin.

segments.chapter: Bands, arranging and other players
segments.title: Bobby the drummer, Black Benny and the break-up of Vincent's band
segments.summary: Vincent says drummer Bobby played with Chris Kelly and then with his band, followed by Black Benny. After Maurice Durant returned from the war and tried to boss the band, it broke up, and he recalls the players joking about age.

segments.chapter: Instruments, singing and technique
segments.title: Bazooka players, Boise and Peewee, and Hudson
segments.summary: Asked about bazooka horns, Vincent remembers two boys, Boise and Peewee, from when he first came down there, and says he remembers Hudson.

segments.chapter: Instruments, singing and technique
segments.title: Penny parties, homemade instruments and the Hesitating Blues
segments.summary: Vincent explains penny parties as lawn parties with homemade instruments such as tin pans and washboards, and asks who played the funny instruments. The talk turns to the Hesitating Blues.

segments.chapter: Instruments, singing and technique
segments.title: Singing: bands rarely had vocalists, and his first song at Audubon Park
segments.summary: Vincent says bands in his day rarely had singers. He first sang Little Liza Jane when a white woman asked him at the Audubon dance, and afterward he kept singing.

segments.chapter: Instruments, singing and technique
segments.title: Why he played chords instead of picking, and switching to banjo
segments.summary: Vincent says he was told picking was too light for the band, so he played chords. He moved from guitar to banjo, learning from Professor Boeese.

segments.chapter: Instruments, singing and technique
segments.title: Taking the first hot chorus with a rap, and the closing thanks
segments.summary: Vincent claims to be the first to take a hot chorus on banjo using a double rap, learned from Julius and perfected with a tin pan behind his banjo. The session ends with thanks.
